This walks one real task end to end: what share of mail ballots were rejected,
by state, in each survey year. It is a common first EAVS analysis, and it has a
trap in it that produces a plausible-looking wrong answer. That trap is the
reason this vignette leads with it rather than saving it for a caveats section.


``` r
library(tidyeavs)

panel <- eavs_load(c(2016, 2018, 2020, 2022, 2024), quiet = TRUE)
dim(panel)
#> [1] 32308    43
```

One row per jurisdiction per year, with harmonized column names. The first call
for a year downloads the published file and caches it; later calls read the
cache.

## Finding the right columns

EAVS variable codes are renumbered between cycles, so the concept names are what
you work with. `eavs_items()` searches the crosswalk both ways:


``` r
eavs_items("mail_rejected")[, c("year", "code", "codebook_label")]
#> # A tibble: 5 × 3
#>    year code  codebook_label                          
#>   <int> <chr> <chr>                                   
#> 1  2016 C4b   C4b. Absentee ballots returned: rejected
#> 2  2018 C4a   By-mail Ballots Rejected: Total         
#> 3  2020 C4a   C4a By-mail Rejected Total              
#> 4  2022 C9a   C9a Mail Rejected Total                 
#> 5  2024 C9a   C9a Total Mail Ballots Rejected
```

The code moves from `C4b` in 2016 to `C4a` in 2018 and 2020, then to `C9a` in
2022 and 2024. Worse, `C4a` means "counted" in 2016 and "drop boxes" in 2022, so
anyone tracking this item by its code across years gets three different
quantities. The `note` column spells out each trap:


``` r
cat(eavs_items("mail_rejected")$note[1])
#> 2016 uses C4b='Absentee ballots returned: rejected'. TRAP: C4b-2018+ ='By-mail Rejected: Deadline' (a rejection REASON, not the total).
```

## The rate

Here is the part worth slowing down for. The obvious approach is to sum
rejections by state, sum returns by state, and divide. That is wrong, and it
fails quietly:


``` r
naive <- aggregate(cbind(mail_rejected, mail_returned) ~ state_abbr,
                   data = subset(panel, year == 2022), FUN = sum, na.rm = TRUE,
                   na.action = na.pass)
naive$rate <- 100 * naive$mail_rejected / naive$mail_returned
naive[naive$state_abbr %in% c("AL", "GA", "VI"), ]
#>    state_abbr mail_rejected mail_returned     rate
#> 2          AL             0         24676 0.000000
#> 12         GA          3785        252272 1.500365
#> 50         VI             0           463 0.000000
```

Alabama and the Virgin Islands both read exactly 0.0%, and only one of them
means it. No Alabama jurisdiction reported rejections that year, so its
numerator is a sum of nothing, and summing nothing gives zero rather than
"unknown". The Virgin Islands really did report, and really did reject none of
their 463 returned ballots. The two are indistinguishable in that table, which
is the problem: a phantom zero and a real zero print identically.

Sometimes the same problem announces itself instead. In 2024 both Alabama and
Connecticut report rejections but no returns, so the division is by zero:


``` r
n24 <- aggregate(cbind(mail_rejected, mail_returned) ~ state_abbr,
                 data = subset(panel, year == 2024), FUN = sum, na.rm = TRUE,
                 na.action = na.pass)
n24$rate <- 100 * n24$mail_rejected / n24$mail_returned
n24[n24$state_abbr %in% c("AL", "CT"), ]
#>   state_abbr mail_rejected mail_returned rate
#> 2         AL          1779             0  Inf
#> 8         CT          2642             0  Inf
```

An `Inf` at least gets noticed. The 0.0% is the one that ends up in a table.
Both come from the same cause: a state can be missing either side of the pair,
and the two sums are computed over different sets of jurisdictions.

`eavs_rate()` restricts each rate to the jurisdictions that reported both sides,
which is how the EAC computes its own published rates:


``` r
rates <- eavs_rate(panel, "mail_rejected", "mail_returned")
head(rates[rates$year == 2022, c("state_abbr", "rate", "n_both", "den_share")], 4)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   state_abbr    rate n_both den_share
#>   <chr>        <dbl>  <int>     <dbl>
#> 1 AK          0.0137      1     1    
#> 2 AL         NA           0     0    
#> 3 AR          0.0706     67     0.957
#> 4 AS         NA           0    NA
```

And the two zeros separate:


``` r
rates[rates$year == 2022 & rates$state_abbr %in% c("AL", "VI"),
      c("state_abbr", "rate", "n_both", "n_num_only", "n_den_only")]
#> # A tibble: 2 × 5
#>   state_abbr  rate n_both n_num_only n_den_only
#>   <chr>      <dbl>  <int>      <int>      <int>
#> 1 AL            NA      0          0         67
#> 2 VI             0      1          0          0
```

Alabama gets no rate at all, and `n_den_only` says why: 67 jurisdictions
reported a denominator with no numerator to divide into it. The Virgin Islands
keep their zero, earned by the one jurisdiction that answered both questions.
Same printed number in the naive table, different facts, and now visibly so.

## Two columns to read before quoting a number

`n_both` is how many jurisdictions stand behind the rate. `den_share` is how
much of the state's reported returned ballots those jurisdictions hold. Both
matter, because a rate computed from two jurisdictions prints exactly like one
computed from two hundred:


``` r
thin <- rates[rates$year == 2022 & rates$den_share < 0.10,
              c("state_abbr", "rate", "n_both", "den_share")]
thin[order(thin$den_share), ]
#> # A tibble: 5 × 4
#>   state_abbr     rate n_both den_share
#>   <chr>         <dbl>  <int>     <dbl>
#> 1 AL         NA            0   0      
#> 2 ID          0.00211      2   0.00369
#> 3 <NA>       NA           NA  NA      
#> 4 <NA>       NA           NA  NA      
#> 5 <NA>       NA           NA  NA
```

Idaho's 2022 rate rests on two jurisdictions holding well under 1% of the
state's mail ballots. The number is arithmetically correct and analytically
useless. This is the single most valuable habit when working with EAVS: the rate
and its support are two different facts, and you need both.

## A national series

To pool groups, add up the numerator and denominator and divide once. Averaging
the state rates would weight Wyoming like California:


``` r
national <- aggregate(cbind(num_value, den_value) ~ year, data = rates, FUN = sum)
national$pct <- round(100 * national$num_value / national$den_value, 2)
national[, c("year", "pct")]
#>   year  pct
#> 1 2016 0.96
#> 2 2018 1.42
#> 3 2020 0.80
#> 4 2022 1.52
#> 5 2024 1.21
```

Around 1% in most cycles, dipping in 2020 when a record volume of mail ballots
was returned. That matches the published record, which is the point of checking.

## Before you publish

Two more steps, each with its own vignette. Run `eavs_flags()` on any panel
spanning years: it catches sums that do not reconcile, implausible swings, and
verified statewide reporting anomalies that no arithmetic check can see. And
pass a status frame to `eavs_aggregate()` when you want totals rather than
rates, so you can see how much of each state actually reported.

For this analysis specifically, the states worth a footnote are the ones where
`n_both` is small, `den_share` is low, or `rate` is `NA`. Those are visible in
the output above rather than something you have to know in advance, which is the
whole reason the columns are there.
